name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.29–8.4 gives a set of six things to be known with the Lord and defines each: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; adhyātma is own being (svabhāva); karma is the sending-forth (visarga) that brings about beings' states of existence; adhibhūta is the perishable state; adhidaivata is the Person (puruṣa); adhiyajña is the Lord himself here in the body. Those who know him so know him even at the time of departure.

members: adhiyajña = the Lord in the body

name: The Lord's lordly yoga (yogam aiśvaram): beings in him, he not in them

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 9.4–6 with 7.12: all this is pervaded by the Lord in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them; and yet beings do not abide in him — 'behold my lordly yoga'; sustaining beings and bringing them into being, his self does not abide in them; as the great wind moving everywhere abides in space, so all beings abide in him. States of the guṇas are from him, he not in them, they in him.

notes: New concept for the Gītā's own phrase (9.5). Extractor A's cpt:aisvara-yoga and extractor B's cpt:yogam-aisvaram are merged under A's id (the stem form of the phrase). The text leaves the paradox of 9.4–5 (beings in him, and yet not in him) unresolved; the commentators' resolutions are recorded in the notes of the teaching 9.5.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.3, 8.11, 8.13, 8.20–21: brahman is the supreme imperishable; it is the akṣara of which the knowers of the Veda speak, which passionless ascetics enter and for which people practise brahmacarya; Oṃ is the one-syllable brahman; the eternal unmanifest beyond the unmanifest is called the akṣara, the highest goal, from which there is no return, the Lord's supreme abode.

Bhagavad Gītā 9.11 with 7.24–25 (the word avatāra is not used): the deluded disregard the Lord who has taken on a human body, not knowing his supreme state as great lord of beings; he is unborn and imperishable, veiled by his yoga-māyā and not manifest to all.

name: Bondage of action (karma-bandha)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord's acts of sending forth beings do not bind (nibadhnanti) him, seated as one indifferent and unattached to them (9.9); whatever one does, eats, offers, gives or practises as austerity, done as an offering to the Lord, frees one from the bonds of action (karma-bandhana) with their good and bad fruits, and, yoked in the yoga of renunciation, freed, one comes to him (9.27–28).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, including extractor B's obstacle entry obs:karma-bondage (9.28).

name: Creation and dissolution of the world

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord is the origin and dissolution of the whole world (7.6; 9.18); at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his prakṛti (9.7–8); prakṛti brings forth the moving and unmoving with him as overseer (9.10); manifest things arise from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night (8.18–19). These acts do not bind him (9.9).

name: The day and night of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand ages and his night likewise; at the coming of day all manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it; the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. Even Brahmā's world is a world of return (8.16).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's entry and extractor B's cpt:ages-and-day-of-brahma (the Gītā does not give the ages or the Manu-periods).

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.15; 9.11–13: evil-doers who have resorted to a demonic disposition (āsura bhāva) do not take refuge in the Lord; those who disregard him in human form, of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras; the great souls resort to the divine nature (daivī prakṛti) and worship him with undivided mind.

Bhagavad Gītā 7 and 9 (without the word prasāda): the Lord makes the worshipper's faith unwavering and ordains the fruits obtained (7.21–22); for the undivided devotee he himself carries acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) (9.22); for the constant rememberer he is easy to reach (8.14).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.16–19: four kinds of people of good deeds worship the Lord — the afflicted (ārta), the one who seeks to know (jijñāsu), the seeker of an object/wealth (arthārthin) and the knower (jñānin). All are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and of single devotion (eka-bhakti), is distinguished: he is exceedingly dear to the Lord and the Lord to him, and is held to be the Lord's very self; at the end of many births he takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' — a great soul very hard to find.

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord announces knowledge together with vijñāna, after which nothing further remains to be known (7.2), and declares it again as the most secret (guhyatama) knowledge to Arjuna, who does not cavil (anasūyu) (9.1); it is the royal knowledge and the royal secret, the supreme purifier, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise and imperishable (9.2); those without faith in this dharma do not reach the Lord (9.3).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's cpt:gita-transmission and extractor B's cpt:secrecy-and-eligibility (9.1–3).

name: Iṣṭāpūrta, merit of sacrifice and gift

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.28, 9.20–21: the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts wins heaven, is exhausted, and brings return to the mortal world; the yogin who knows the teaching passes beyond all such merit to the supreme primal place.

notes: The word iṣṭāpūrta does not occur in the Gītā; 8.28 speaks of the fruit of merit (puṇya-phala) declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts, and 9.20–21 of the merit that wins heaven and is spent.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 9.9–10: the acts of sending forth beings do not bind the Lord, who sits as if indifferent, unattached to them; prakṛti gives birth to the moving and unmoving with him as overseer.
Bhagavad Gītā 7.5: the Lord's higher nature 'has become the living being' (jīvabhūtā) and upholds the world.

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.17, 9.7–8: the day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas and his night likewise (8.17); at the end of a kalpa all beings go into the Lord's prakṛti, and at the beginning of a kalpa he, taking hold of his own prakṛti, sends forth again the whole multitude of beings, helpless under prakṛti's power (9.7–8).

name: The last thought at death

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.5–7: whoever departs remembering the Lord alone at the time of the end comes to his state; whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having always been shaped by it; therefore one should remember him at all times (and, for Arjuna, fight).

relations.note: the yogin's form of the last remembrance (8.10–13)

notes: The ch01-03 merge linked 2.72 ('even at the time of the end') to cpt:last-thought; the Gītā unit's cpt:last-thought-at-death, used here by both extractors, covers 8.5–7 (flagged for the S5 dedupe review).

name: Liberation

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: those who take refuge in the Lord and strive for release (mokṣa) from old age and death know Brahman, the adhyātma and action completely (7.29); the great souls who come to him, having reached the highest perfection, do not come to rebirth, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return (8.15–16); the imperishable unmanifest, the supreme goal and the Lord's supreme abode, is that from which those who reach it do not return (8.21); departing by the bright course, knowers of Brahman go to Brahman — the course of non-return (anāvṛtti) (8.23–24, 8.26); offering every act to the Lord, one is freed (vimukta) from the bonds of action and comes to him (9.28).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution; the non-return side of extractor B's cpt:punaravrtti-anavrtti.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.14–15, 7.25: the Lord's divine māyā, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross; those who take refuge in him alone cross it; it carries off the knowledge of evil-doers; veiled by his yoga-māyā the Lord is not manifest to all.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the Lord is the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8) and the oṃkāra along with the three Vedas (9.17); Oṃ is 'the one-syllabled Brahman', uttered at departure while remembering the Lord (8.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 7.26: the Lord knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him.

name: Rebirth

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs (7.27); the knower takes refuge in the Lord at the end of many births (7.19); one goes to whatever state one remembers on leaving the body (8.6); rebirth is the impermanent abode of sorrow, and all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return, but those who come to the Lord are not reborn (8.15–16); the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly, with Brahmā's day and night (8.19); of the two everlasting courses of the departed, the bright leads to non-return (anāvṛtti) and the dark to return (8.23–26); those without faith in this dharma return to the path of death and saṃsāra (9.3); Vedic sacrificers who reach heaven re-enter the world of mortals when their merit is spent — 'going and coming' (9.21).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's cpt:rebirth and extractor B's cpt:punaravrtti-anavrtti (return and non-return); the non-return side is also recorded under cpt:liberation.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.21–22; 9.3, 9.23: whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that faith unwavering, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by the Lord; those without faith in this dharma return to saṃsāra; devotees of other deities worship with faith, and so worship the Lord, but not according to rule.

name: Surrender to the Lord (śaraṇāgati / prapatti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.14, 7.19, 7.29; 9.32: those who take refuge in the Lord alone cross his guṇa-made māyā; the knower takes refuge after many births knowing 'Vāsudeva is all'; those who take refuge strive for release from old age and death; whoever takes refuge — even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras — reaches the highest goal. Evil-doers of demonic disposition do not take refuge (7.15).

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor A's cpt:surrender-to-the-lord and extractor B's cpt:prapatti. The verbs are pra-√pad (7.14, 7.15, 7.19, 7.20), ā-√śri (7.29) and vy-apa-ā-√śri (9.32).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 9.20–21: those versed in the three Vedas, soma-drinkers purified of sin, worship with sacrifices and pray for heaven; they reach the world of the lord of the gods and enjoy the gods' divine pleasures, but when their merit is exhausted they re-enter the world of mortals — 'going and coming'. 8.16: the worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return.

Bhagavad Gītā 7.12–14: states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from the Lord, he not in them but they in him; the world, deluded by these three guṇa-made states, does not know him who is beyond them; his divine māyā is made of the guṇas.

name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7.4–7: the Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I' (ahaṅkāra); his higher nature has become the living being and upholds the world. All beings have these two as their source; he is the origin and dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all is strung on him like gems on a thread.

members: parā prakṛti jīvabhūtā (the higher nature, become the living being)

name: The two paths after death (bright and dark)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 8.23–27: the two perennial courses of departing yogins — the bright (śukla): fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course, by which knowers of brahman go to brahman and do not return; and the dark (kṛṣṇa): smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course, by which the yogin reaches the lunar light and returns. Knowing the two paths, the yogin is not deluded.

members: śukla gati: agni, jyotis, ahaḥ, śukla pakṣa, uttarāyaṇa → brahman, anāvṛtti (8.24, 8.26)
kṛṣṇa gati: dhūma, rātri, kṛṣṇa pakṣa, dakṣiṇāyana → cāndramasaṃ jyotiḥ, āvṛtti (8.25–26)

names.name: śukla-kṛṣṇe gatī (the bright and dark courses, 8.26); sṛtī (the two paths, 8.27)

notes: Chs. 7–9 contribution, combining extractor B's entry and extractor A's cpt:devayana-pitryana. The Gītā does not use the Upaniṣadic names devayāna and pitṛyāna; its stations parallel Chāndogya 5.10.1–6 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2.15–16 (the Upaniṣadic doctrine is cpt:devayana-pitryana; flagged for the S5 dedupe/equivalence review).

name: Varṇa — the four classes, as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 9.32–33: taking refuge in the Lord, even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal — how much more holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers.

Bhagavad Gītā 7.8–11 and 9.16–19 (the word vibhūti itself is not used in these verses): the Lord is the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, pure fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendour of the splendid, strength free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; and the rite, the sacrifice, the offering, the fire and the oblation, father, mother, sustainer and grandfather of the world, Oṃ and the three Vedas, goal, witness, refuge and friend, immortality and death, sat and asat.

Bhagavad Gītā 7.24; 8.18–21; 9.4: manifest things come forth from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night; beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest which does not perish when beings perish, called the akṣara, the highest goal and the Lord's supreme abode; the Lord pervades the world in unmanifest form; the unintelligent think him, the unmanifest, to have come into manifestation.

Bhagavad Gītā 9.15–16, 9.24, 9.26–27: some worship the Lord by the sacrifice of knowledge; he is the rite, the sacrifice, the ancestral offering, the herb, the mantra, the butter, the fire and the oblation; he is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices; a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered in devotion he accepts; every act, eating, oblation, gift and austerity is to be done as an offering to him.

Bhagavad Gītā 8.10–13: at the time of departure the yogin, with unmoving mind, devotion and the power of yoga, makes the breath enter between the brows and reaches the supreme divine Person; restraining all the gates, confining the mind in the heart, placing the breath in the head, established in yogic concentration, uttering Oṃ and remembering the Lord, he goes to the supreme goal.
